 NE Oregon has strongest earthquake in more than 30 years
 Published 8:00 pm Friday, November 13, 2026
 By Jayson Jacoby | Baker City Herald

 JOSEPH — A small earthquake, albeit the strongest in Northeastern Oregon in more than 30 years, hit late Nov. 9 in Wallowa County southeast of Joseph.
 The quake, recorded at 11:43 p.m., had a magnitude of 4.3, according to Pacific Northwest Seismic Network.
 The epicenter was near Carrol Creek, a tributary of Big Sheep Creek about 3 miles east of the Wallowa Mountain Loop Road and about 12 miles southeast of Joseph. The quake happened about 7.5 miles underground (the initial report stated 1.5 miles).
 Doug Gibbons, seismic lab coordinator for the Pacific Northwest Seismic Network, said based on the network’s historical database, the temblor was the strongest in Northeastern Oregon since a magnitude 4.0 quake on Oct. 27, 1994, about 7 miles southeast of Halfway.
 Gibbons said the quake was slightly too weak to trigger a public notice, through cellphone messages similar to Amber Alerts, through the ShakeAlert system.
 The threshold for ShakeAlert is magnitude 4.5, Gibbons said.
 The epicenter was along the Wallowa Fault, which geologists have mapped for at least 31 miles along the base of the Wallowas from near Highway 82 west of Wallowa, where the highway enters the Wallowa River Canyon, southeast past Wallowa Lake to near McCully Creek southeast of the lake. 
 Gibbons said the fault extends farther, although the epicenter for the quake is on a section of the fault that hasn’t been mapped.
 The Wallowa Fault is one of the longer faults in Northeastern Oregon, Gibbons said. The Wallowas, which tower above Wallowa Valley, resulted in part from uplifting along the fault, he said.
 Similar faults run along both the east and west sides of the Grande Ronde Valley, and on the west side of Baker Valley along the base of the Elkhorns.
 Other past quakes in the area include a magnitude 3.0 temblor on Nov. 6, 2002, about 2 miles southeast of the epicenter of the Nov. 9 quake, a magnitude 3.0 on March 3, 1999, near the junction of the Imnaha Highway and the Wallowa Mountain Road, and a 3.3 on Nov. 4, 2014, about 3 miles east of Joseph.
 As of Nov. 12, no aftershocks had been recorded in the area, according to the U.S. Geological Survey. The agency listed a 20% chance for an aftershock of at least magnitude 3.0 within a week of the Nov. 9 quake, and a 3% chance of an aftershock of at least magnitude 4.0.
 Dozens of reports from residents
 According to the U.S. Geological Survey, esidents in parts of Wallowa, Baker and Union counties, including near Baker City and Halfway could have felt “weak” or “light” shaking from the quake.
 The federal agency had 98 reports from people who felt the quake as of 10 a.m. Nov. 10, including from Enterprise, Joseph, Imnaha, North Powder, La Grande, Halfway and Union. 
 Gibbons said he’s not surprised by the number of reports. A magnitude 4.3 quake is strong enough to be felt even many miles from the epicenter, he said, but that magnitude typically is too low to cause damage.
 The USGS projects a “low likelihood” for damage.
 The epicenter was in a relatively remote area within the Wallowa-Whitman National Forest.
 The USGS reports include estimates for the Modified Mercalli Intensity scale, which measures the intensity of shaking (a different measurement than the magnitude). According to the citizen reports, the intensity ranged from level 3, which is “weak,” to level 4, which is “light.”
 Residents talk about their experiences
 Sheila Orr, who lives about halfway between Enterprise and Joseph, said she was asleep when the quake started.
 Orr said she’s not sure whether the shaking, or her bulldog, woke her up, but when she did an antique dresser was shaking.
 Orr, who was in Willamette Valley during the 1993 “spring break” quake, said she immediately thought of an earthquake.
 There was no damage and she said she went back to sleep.
 When she woke up Nov. 10 she saw social media posts about the quake.
 Orr said she talked with two friends who live in Joseph and both slept through the quake.
 Gibbons said the seismic network’s automatic detection system “did a fantastic job” determining the epicenter almost immediately and coming up with a magnitude estimate within about four minutes.
 Kristen Ruckdashel, who lives in Enterprise, appreciated the rapid reporting after her house shook for a few seconds, leaving her to wonder “what could that possibly have been?”
 Ruckdashel, who was awake at the time, said her first thought was that a herd of elk had lumbered through her yard. But she said there was none of the rustling noises she associates with thudding hooves, and when she looked outside she saw no animals.
 Ruckdashel said she checked online and saw the report about the quake.
 She also posted on her FB page, and quickly had responses from friends who also felt the quake.
 Ruckdashel, who grew up in Enterprise and graduated from Enterprise High School in 1991, said the temblor was her first.
 “It was amazing,” she said.
 The shaking knocked over a few bottles in her bathroom but didn’t cause any damage, she said.
 Emily Glock, who lives between Baker City and Durkee, said she had just gone to bed after working late when the nightstand beside the bed shook, rattling the items on it.
 Glock said she at first thought her husband, Dylan, who was working in their shop, had come inside and shut the door.
 She said she looked at the clock and remembered it showed 11:43 p.m.
 When she woke up Nov. 10 she saw a Facebook post about the quake and realized what she had felt the night before.
 Glock said her husband didn’t feel anything while he was working in the shop.
 She said she grew up in California and, while living in Truckee, near Lake Tahoe, she was in an earthquake that dislodged dishes from a cabinet.
 Columbia Basin survey and NE Oregon’s biggest recorded quake
 Lalo Guerrero, a geology hazard specialist for the Oregon Department of Geology and Mineral Industries. has been studying the geology, and earthquake hazards, in an area of the Columbia Basin from east of Milton-Freewater west and northwest to the Columbia River near Wallula Gap. The study area covers 50-70 square miles.
 The area includes the fault near Milton-Freewater that produced Northeast Oregon’s most powerful recorded quake. It happened at 11:08 p.m. on July 15, 1936, and was recorded at 17 seismographs. Geologists estimate the magnitude at 6.1.
 The quake, which was followed by four significant aftershocks, on July 18, Aug. 4 and Aug. 28, caused major damage in Milton-Freewater, Umapine and Stateline.
 Shaking damaged chimneys, shifted homes off their foundations and caused damage estimated at $100,000, according to DOGAMI documents.
 The quake also caused the ground to crack in many places, some of which were several feet wide. In one place the ground dropped by nearly 10 feet.
 Guerrero said the current study examines faults in the area, known as the Wallula fault zone, in greater detail than ever before.
